香之氣始芬然而升，上帝之神已居然面饗也。何但芳臭之薦信得其時哉？蓋自后稷以農功而受封，因稼穡而肇祀，則庶無罪悔，以至于今矣。然則天應之疾者有由然也，豈徒以其物哉？抑觀此詩與《思文》均爲尊稷配天作也，而詳畧不同，何耶？蓋此爲序事宜詳，不詳無以見其始終；彼爲獻詞宜簡，不簡無以見其嚴肅。讀詩者不可不知。

translation_en:
…the fragrant vapors have only just begun to rise, yet the spirit of the Lord on High is already manifestly present to receive the offerings. How could this mean merely that the fragrant offerings were indeed presented at the proper time? Since Hou Ji received his fief for his achievements in agriculture and instituted sacrifices through his cultivation of grain, there has been, one may hope, no transgression or cause for regret down to the present. Thus Heaven has reason to respond so swiftly: could it be solely on account of the offerings themselves? Furthermore, this ode and “Si Wen” (The Cultured One) were both composed to honor Hou Ji by associating him with Heaven in sacrifice. Why, then, does their degree of detail differ? This ode narrates events and therefore calls for detail; without detail, it could not show their course from beginning to end. The other provides words of presentation and therefore calls for brevity; without brevity, it could not convey solemn reverence. Readers of the Odes must understand this.
“I present my offerings: sheep and oxen. May Heaven aid us.”

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
明堂也盖有其誠則有其神也周王奉祭而□□
天之降監其大享之誠何如哉此宗祀文王於
明堂以配上帝之樂歌吾想周王於季秋之月
行大享之禮而以父配帝意豈不曰我所奉於
明堂之上以享上帝者果何物耶少牢之羊可
以為俎實也則維羊之是奉于以盡宗祀之誠
焉我所薦於明堂之間以享上帝者又何物耶
太牢之牛可以為犧牲也則維牛之是薦于以
===
行大享之禮焉然維羊之奉特以將吾誠爾彼
皇皇后帝巍巍在上也庶其有感而在此羊之
右乎維牛之薦特以行吾禮爾彼浩浩昊天高
高在上也庶其俯降而在此牛之右乎曰其右
之者蓋不敢必也周人明堂之祭尊尊之意有
如是夫載觀思文之頌旣尊后稷以配天矣此
又尊文王以配帝何耶盖萬物本乎天人本乎
祖故冬至祭天而以祖配之所以尊尊也萬物
punctuated: 明堂也。盖有其誠，則有其神也。周王奉祭而□□天之降監，其大享之誠何如哉！此宗祀文王於明堂，以配上帝之樂歌。吾想周王於季秋之月，行大享之禮而以父配帝，意豈不曰：「我所奉於明堂之上以享上帝者，果何物耶？少牢之羊，可以為俎實也，則維羊之是奉，于以盡宗祀之誠焉。我所薦於明堂之間以享上帝者，又何物耶？太牢之牛，可以為犧牲也，則維牛之是薦，于以行大享之禮焉。然維羊之奉，特以將吾誠爾。彼皇皇后帝，巍巍在上也，庶其有感而在此羊之右乎！維牛之薦，特以行吾禮爾。彼浩浩昊天，高高在上也，庶其俯降而在此牛之右乎！」曰「其右之」者，蓋不敢必也。周人明堂之祭，尊尊之意有如是夫！載觀《思文》之頌，旣尊后稷以配天矣，此又尊文王以配帝，何耶？盖萬物本乎天，人本乎祖，故冬至祭天而以祖配之，所以尊尊也。萬物
translation_en:
…the Hall of Light. For where there is sincerity, there is the presence of the spirits. The king of Zhou presents his sacrifices and [two illegible characters: ?] Heaven’s descent to look upon them: how profound is his sincerity in this great offering! This is the ritual song for sacrificing to King Wen in the Hall of Light as the correlate of the Lord on High. I imagine that when the king of Zhou performed the rite of the great offering in the last month of autumn, making his father the correlate of the Lord on High, his thoughts must have been these: “What, indeed, do I present in the Hall of Light as an offering to the Lord on High? The sheep of the lesser sacrifice can fill the sacrificial stand; thus it is a sheep that I present, fully expressing my sincerity in this ancestral sacrifice. What else do I offer within the Hall of Light to the Lord on High? The ox of the greater sacrifice can serve as a sacrificial victim; thus it is an ox that I offer, thereby performing the rite of the great offering.

“Yet presenting the sheep serves only to convey my sincerity. That resplendent Sovereign Lord towers majestically above: may he respond and be here at the right of this sheep! Offering the ox serves only to carry out my ritual observance. That vast, expansive Heaven is high above: may he descend and be here at the right of this ox!” The words “may he be at their right” express his unwillingness to presume that this will surely happen. Such was the Zhou people’s intention of honoring the exalted in their sacrifice at the Hall of Light!

“Cultured One” (Siwen), the sacrificial hymn, shows that they already honored Hou Ji as the correlate of Heaven. Why, then, do they here also honor King Wen as the correlate of the Lord on High? All things have their origin in Heaven, and human beings have their origin in their ancestors. Thus, at the winter solstice they sacrifice to Heaven with their ancestor as its correlate: this is how they honor the exalted. All things…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭鄭批措詞簡當
考試官學正朱批發明重民力之意可嘉
役民而非時害義者春秋固著其罪役民而雖
時且義者春秋亦重其事此可見民力不可以
輕而用之也何則爲民立君所以養之也養民
之道在愛其力今我魯隱當國七年夏也而有
中丘之城九年夏也又有郎邑之築是二城也
正農事之方殷勞民力於興作是使民非時矣
===
桓公懼齊鄭之襲紀而有祝丘之城莊公恐納
糾之見討亦有洙水之浚是二役也弗脩德以
禦患惟恃險以自防是使民害義矣夫使民不
時害義則民力不足生養不遂豈君國子民之
道哉故春秋必歷書以著其罪也若夫莊公城
諸防也乃龍見戒事之時宣公城平陽也於火
見致用之日之二城也當三務之始畢正百穀
之告成是使民得其時矣仲孫從晉定有成周
punctuated:
考試官敎諭鄭批：措詞簡當。

考試官學正朱批：發明重民力之意，可嘉。

役民而非時害義者，春秋固著其罪；役民而雖時且義者，春秋亦重其事。此可見民力不可以輕而用之也。何則？爲民立君，所以養之也。養民之道，在愛其力。今我魯隱當國七年夏也，而有中丘之城；九年夏也，又有郎邑之築。是二城也，正農事之方殷，勞民力於興作，是使民非時矣。

桓公懼齊鄭之襲紀，而有祝丘之城；莊公恐納糾之見討，亦有洙水之浚。是二役也，弗脩德以禦患，惟恃險以自防，是使民害義矣。夫使民不時害義，則民力不足，生養不遂，豈君國子民之道哉？故春秋必歷書以著其罪也。若夫莊公城諸防也，乃龍見戒事之時；宣公城平陽也，於火見致用之日。之二城也，當三務之始畢，正百穀之告成，是使民得其時矣。仲孫從晉定，有成周
translation_en:
Examiner Zheng, Instructor of a County Confucian School, comments: “The wording is concise and apt.”

Examiner Zhu, Instructor of a Subprefectural Confucian School, comments: “Its elucidation of the importance of the people’s labor is commendable.”

When the people are put to work out of season and contrary to righteousness, the Spring and Autumn Annals certainly makes the offense manifest. Yet even when they are put to work in season and in accordance with righteousness, the Annals also treats the undertaking as a weighty matter. This shows that the people’s labor must not be employed lightly. Why is this? A ruler is established for the people in order to nurture them. The way to nurture the people lies in cherishing their strength. Now, in the summer of the seventh year of Duke Yin’s rule over our state of Lu, there was the walling of Zhongqiu; in the summer of his ninth year, there was also the fortification of the town of Lang. Both these wall-building projects took place precisely when agricultural work was at its busiest. To exhaust the people’s strength on construction was to employ them out of season.

Duke Huan feared that Qi and Zheng would attack Ji, and so undertook the walling of Zhuqiu. Duke Zhuang feared punitive action for his attempt to install Jiu, and likewise undertook the dredging of the Zhu River. In these two undertakings, instead of cultivating virtue to ward off calamity, they relied solely on defensive barriers to protect themselves. This was to employ the people contrary to righteousness. When the people are employed out of season and contrary to righteousness, their strength is depleted and they cannot secure their livelihoods and support their families. How could this be the way to rule a state and care for its people as one’s children? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals necessarily records each undertaking to make the offense manifest. As for Duke Zhuang’s walling of Fang, this occurred when the Dragon asterism appeared, the time to give notice of the work; Duke Xuan’s walling of Pingyang occurred when the Fire star appeared, the time to put labor to use. These two wall-building projects took place just as the three seasonal agricultural tasks had been completed and the various grains had reached maturity. This was to employ the people at the proper time. Zhongsun followed Duke Ding of Jin, and there was the undertaking at Chengzhou …

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之城魯定命叔季有郈費之墮之三役也供臣
職以藩王室張公室以弱私家是使民合乎義
矣夫使民雖時且義豈能免營築力役之勞哉
故春秋亦備書以重其事也吁不時害義固爲
罪雖時且義而亦書非以見勞民爲重事矣乎
大抵民惟邦本本固邦寧故固國以保民爲本
人君能愛民力而民力足則生養遂敎化行風
俗美而邦本固矣使不能愛民而輕用民力於
===
守國之末務則邦本一搖雖有城池之固誰與
之守此春秋於用民力必書以爲重也噫人君
而知此義則知慎重於用民力矣
公會宰周公齊侯宋子衛侯鄭伯許男曹
伯于葵丘諸侯盟于葵丘〔僖公九年〕宋

punctuated:
之城，魯定命叔季有郈費之墮。之三役也，供臣職以藩王室，張公室以弱私家，是使民合乎義矣。夫使民雖時且義，豈能免營築力役之勞哉？故《春秋》亦備書以重其事也。吁！不時害義，固爲罪；雖時且義而亦書，非以見勞民爲重事矣乎？大抵民惟邦本，本固邦寧，故固國以保民爲本。人君能愛民力而民力足，則生養遂，敎化行，風俗美，而邦本固矣。使不能愛民，而輕用民力於守國之末務，則邦本一搖，雖有城池之固，誰與之守？此《春秋》於用民力必書以爲重也。噫！人君而知此義，則知慎重於用民力矣。

translation_en:
…the construction of the wall. Duke Ding of Lu commanded Shu and Ji to demolish the walls of Hou and Fei. These three undertakings fulfilled the duties of subjects in defending the royal house, and strengthened the ducal house while weakening private lineages: this was employing the people in accordance with righteousness. Yet even when the people are employed at the proper time and for righteous purposes, how can they escape the toil of construction and compulsory labor? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals also records these matters fully, treating them as weighty affairs. Ah! Employing the people at the wrong time and violating righteousness are certainly offenses; but even employment at the proper time and for righteous purposes is recorded. Does this not show that making the people toil is a serious matter?
In general, the people are the foundation of the state; when the foundation is secure, the state is at peace. Thus securing the state must rest upon protecting the people. If a ruler cherishes the people’s strength, so that they have strength enough, they can sustain their livelihoods and rear their families, moral instruction can take effect, customs can improve, and the foundation of the state can become secure. If he cannot cherish the people, but recklessly expends their strength on the secondary tasks of defending the state, then, once its foundation is shaken, who will join him in defending it, however strong its walls and moats? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals invariably records the use of the people’s labor, treating it as a weighty matter. Ah! A ruler who understands this principle will know to exercise care and restraint in employing the people’s strength.

The Duke met with Viscount Liu, the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Xiao Zhu at Pingqiu. They jointly covenanted at Pingqiu. Thirteenth year of Duke Zhao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Assistant Instructor: “The topic is grounded in the meaning of the commentary, which most writers fail to understand, making one weary of reading [?]. This essay recognizes that none of the Five Hegemons surpassed Duke Huan of Qi, and that the other ministers fall short of Minister Kong. Its wording is orderly and ample, and its exposition detailed and clear. Its author must have devoted himself to the Classic of the Unicorn [the Spring and Autumn Annals]. It certainly deserves selection for inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “It does not depart from the meaning of the commentary.”

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Instructor: “The writing and reasoning are pertinent and sound.”

The hegemonic lord and the chief minister both rendered meritorious service to the royal house. The successive hegemons could not sustain that eminence…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
諸臣無以及其賢此可見五伯莫盛於齊桓而
諸臣皆有愧於宰孔也慨自黍離既降雅頌不
作王室之不尊久矣咺賵仲子糾聘桓公王臣
之不賢甚矣所幸齊桓創伯廼心王室合諸侯
爲葵丘之會適宰孔有賜胙之行于時孔也嚴
恭寅畏宣加勞賜級之命桓也俯伏下拜盡天
威咫尺之恭已而宰孔言旋盟禮斯講申五命
之詞示一王之法束牲載書而不歃血桓公之
===
信義以著唯與之會而不與盟宰臣之名分以
尊桓之伯業於斯爲盛孔之奬伯亦與有功厥
後宋晉秦楚接踵而主伯於當時尹單劉子相
繼而下臨於伯國使能蹈芳躅而繼休績則桓
與孔豈得專美於前哉夫何曹南有盟而宋襄
之作舍無成城濮戰楚而晉文則陰謀取勝秦
穆之伐晉也濟河焚舟未免有逞忿之失楚莊
之盟辰陵也假義討罪不過濟貪利之私之數
punctuated: 諸臣無以及其賢。此可見五伯莫盛於齊桓，而諸臣皆有愧於宰孔也。慨自黍離既降，雅頌不作，王室之不尊久矣！咺賵仲子，糾聘桓公，王臣之不賢甚矣！所幸齊桓創伯，廼心王室，合諸侯爲葵丘之會，適宰孔有賜胙之行。于時孔也嚴恭寅畏，宣加勞賜級之命；桓也俯伏下拜，盡天威咫尺之恭。已而宰孔言旋，盟禮斯講，申五命之詞，示一王之法，束牲載書而不歃血，桓公之信義以著。唯與之會而不與盟，宰臣之名分以尊。桓之伯業於斯爲盛，孔之奬伯亦與有功。厥後宋晉秦楚接踵而主伯於當時，尹單劉子相繼而下臨於伯國。使能蹈芳躅而繼休績，則桓與孔豈得專美於前哉？夫何曹南有盟，而宋襄之作舍無成；城濮戰楚，而晉文則陰謀取勝；秦穆之伐晉也，濟河焚舟，未免有逞忿之失；楚莊之盟辰陵也，假義討罪，不過濟貪利之私。之數
translation_en:
…none of the ministers could match his worthiness. From this we can see that none of the Five Hegemons surpassed Duke Huan of Qi, and that all those ministers fell short of Minister Kong. Alas, ever since “Millet Drooping” was relegated to the Airs and the Elegantiae and Eulogies ceased to be composed, the royal house had long gone unhonored! Xuan presented funeral gifts for Zhongzi, and Jiu paid a diplomatic visit to Duke Huan: how unworthy the king’s ministers had become! Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi established his hegemony with his heart devoted to the royal house. He assembled the feudal lords at Kuiqiu, just as Minister Kong was making his journey to bestow sacrificial meat. Kong, solemnly respectful and reverently apprehensive, proclaimed the command conveying special commendation and the bestowal of rank [?]; Huan prostrated himself and bowed below the steps, showing the utmost reverence as though the awesome royal presence were only inches away. After Minister Kong departed on his return journey, the covenant ceremony was performed. The terms of the five injunctions were reiterated, setting forth the laws of the one true king. The sacrificial victim was bound and the covenant recorded, but no blood was smeared upon the lips. Thus Duke Huan’s trustworthiness and righteousness were made manifest. By participating in the assembly but not in the covenant, the royal minister upheld the dignity of his proper station. Huan’s achievement as hegemon reached its height here, and Kong too shared in the merit through his support for the hegemon.

Thereafter, Song, Jin, Qin, and Chu successively exercised hegemony in their day, while the lords of Yin, Shan, and Liu came down in succession to the hegemonic states. Had they followed those admirable footsteps and continued those splendid achievements, how could Huan and Kong alone have enjoyed the glory of their earlier deeds? Yet why was it that, when a covenant was made south of Cao, Duke Xiang of Song accomplished nothing, like a man building a house amid conflicting advice; that, in fighting Chu at Chengpu, Duke Wen of Jin won by covert stratagems; that Duke Mu of Qin, in attacking Jin, crossed the Yellow River and burned his boats, failing to avoid the fault of indulging his anger; and that Duke Zhuang of Chu, in making the covenant at Chenling, invoked righteousness to punish wrongdoing but merely gratified his selfish greed for advantage? These several [?] …

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
君者雖雄長於一時其於世道何補回視齊桓
之尊王室明五禁以一匡天下豈可同日語哉
伐鄭盟柯陵也而晉厲則瀆尹武單襄以講信
雞澤謀外楚也而晉悼復扳單頃公以要言晉
昭因懼楚為平丘之會盟劉獻亦屈己以同事
於牲歃之數子者瀆尊卑之大分則於君命有
辱回視宰孔之獎伯主謹名分以表正天下豈
可一例觀哉故春秋備書則其優劣賢否自見
===
矣雖然齊桓固為五伯之盛然自葵丘之後伯
業漸衰何有王者不息之誠宰孔固為諸臣之
賢然前此阿順王命撫鄭從楚何有大臣格君
之道合而觀之則桓孔之功過得失不可掩矣
禮記
德盛而教尊五穀時熟然後賞之以樂
陸中行
同考試官訓導左批勤於治民則德盛應氏
punctuated:
君者，雖雄長於一時，其於世道何補？回視齊桓之尊王室、明五禁，以一匡天下，豈可同日語哉？伐鄭盟柯陵也，而晉厲則瀆尹武、單襄以講信；雞澤謀外楚也，而晉悼復扳單頃公以要言；晉昭因懼楚為平丘之會盟，劉獻亦屈己以同事於牲歃。之數子者，瀆尊卑之大分，則於君命有辱。回視宰孔之獎伯主、謹名分，以表正天下，豈可一例觀哉？故《春秋》備書，則其優劣賢否自見矣。雖然，齊桓固為五伯之盛，然自葵丘之後，伯業漸衰，何有王者不息之誠？宰孔固為諸臣之賢，然前此阿順王命，撫鄭從楚，何有大臣格君之道？合而觀之，則桓、孔之功過得失不可掩矣。
《禮記》
德盛而教尊，五穀時熟，然後賞之以樂。
陸中行
同考試官訓導左批：勤於治民則德盛，應氏
translation_en:
…these rulers, though dominant in their own times, contributed what to the moral order of the world? Looking back at Duke Huan of Qi, who honored the royal house and clarified the five prohibitions, thereby setting all under Heaven right, how could they be spoken of in the same breath? When Zheng was attacked and the covenant made at Keling, Duke Li of Jin demeaned Duke Wu of Yin and Duke Xiang of Shan by having them pledge good faith. When plans were made at Jize to exclude Chu, Duke Dao of Jin again drew Duke Qing of Shan into a sworn agreement. Duke Zhao of Jin, fearing Chu, convened the covenant assembly at Pingqiu, and Duke Xian of Liu likewise lowered himself to participate in the sacrificial and blood-oath rites. These men [?] violated the fundamental distinction between superior and inferior, thereby dishonoring their sovereign’s commission. Looking back at Zai Kong, who supported the hegemon and carefully upheld distinctions of status to set an example and rectify all under Heaven, how could they be judged alike? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records everything fully, and their relative merits and worth become apparent of themselves.
Nevertheless, although Duke Huan of Qi was indeed the foremost of the Five Hegemons, his hegemonic enterprise gradually declined after Kuiqiu. Where was the unceasing sincerity of a true king? Although Zai Kong was indeed a worthy minister, he had earlier compliantly followed the king’s commands, pacifying Zheng and following Chu. Where was the great minister’s way of correcting his ruler? Considered together, the achievements and faults, successes and failures of Huan and Kong cannot be concealed.
Record of Rites
“When their virtue is abundant and their teaching held in honor, and the five grains ripen in season, only then are they rewarded with music.”
Lu Zhongxing
Comment by Associate Examiner Zuo, Assistant Instructor: “Diligence in governing the people makes virtue abundant. Master Ying’s…”

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之註作者昧此臆說紛紛惟此篇認理詳明措詞典
雅其禮經之翹楚者乎
考試官教諭鄭批說出天子以樂賞諸侯之意
宛然在目
考試官學正朱批詞簡意足禮經無出其右者
人臣德懋而有其驗人君必錫以章德之具也
夫樂所以章德也人臣德懋而有其驗如此人
君得不賞之以樂哉記樂記者謂夫昔天子之
===
爲樂將以賞諸侯之有德者也彼爲之諸侯者
勤於教民而勞來匡直之匪懈勤於養民而勸
課巡行之不怠非有德而勤於爲治者不能也
然勤於教民而教道未尊未見其德之盛也必
若父子有親君臣有義與夫夫婦長幼朋友之
教民皆承聽而無敢慢易則德之盛於此乎可
驗勤於養民而五穀未熟亦未見其德之盛也
必若麥熟於夏稻熟於秋與夫若黍若稷若菽
punctuated:
之註，作者昧此，臆說紛紛。惟此篇認理詳明，措詞典雅，其禮經之翹楚者乎！
考試官教諭鄭批：說出天子以樂賞諸侯之意，宛然在目。
考試官學正朱批：詞簡意足，禮經無出其右者。
人臣德懋而有其驗，人君必錫以章德之具也。
夫樂所以章德也。人臣德懋而有其驗如此，人君得不賞之以樂哉？記《樂記》者謂夫昔天子之爲樂，將以賞諸侯之有德者也。彼爲之諸侯者，勤於教民，而勞來匡直之匪懈；勤於養民，而勸課巡行之不怠，非有德而勤於爲治者不能也。然勤於教民而教道未尊，未見其德之盛也。必若父子有親，君臣有義，與夫夫婦、長幼、朋友之教，民皆承聽而無敢慢易，則德之盛於此乎可驗。勤於養民而五穀未熟，亦未見其德之盛也。必若麥熟於夏，稻熟於秋，與夫若黍、若稷、若菽
translation_en:
…’s annotation. Writers fail to grasp this, and speculative explanations abound. This essay alone apprehends the principles clearly and thoroughly, expressing them in elegant, classical language. Surely it is among the finest essays on the Classic of Rites!
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: The intention behind the Son of Heaven’s rewarding the feudal lords with music is explained so vividly that it seems present before our eyes.
Comment by Examiner Zhu, School Instructor: Concise in wording and complete in meaning; among essays on the Classic of Rites, none surpasses it.
When a subject’s virtue flourishes and there is evidence of it, his ruler will surely bestow upon him the means to display that virtue.
Music is the means by which virtue is displayed. When a subject’s virtue flourishes and is attested in this way, how could his ruler fail to reward him with music? The author of the Record of Music says that when the Son of Heaven in antiquity instituted music, he intended thereby to reward those feudal lords who possessed virtue. Those serving as feudal lords diligently instructed the people, tirelessly encouraging, drawing them to good, correcting, and guiding them; they diligently provided for the people’s livelihood, untiringly exhorting and supervising them and making inspection tours. Only those who possessed virtue and worked diligently at governing could accomplish this.
Yet if they diligently instructed the people but their teachings were not honored, the fullness of their virtue would not yet be evident. Only when there was affection between father and son, righteousness between ruler and subject, and instruction concerning husband and wife, elder and younger, and friends—and the people all accepted and obeyed, none daring to treat these teachings lightly—could the fullness of their virtue be verified in this.
If they diligently provided for the people’s livelihood but the five grains did not ripen, the fullness of their virtue would likewise not yet be evident. Only when wheat ripened in summer and rice in autumn, together with such crops as broomcorn millet, foxtail millet, and beans…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之類各以時熟而無或愆期則德之盛於此乎
可徵天子於此得不賞樂以章其德哉盖樂有
羽旄夔所制也于焉錫之以羽旄以為文舞之
用樂有干戚夔所制也于焉錫之以干戚以充
武舞之列是則樂舞一舉而侯德以著綴兆一
陳而侯德以章先王賞樂於諸侯豈苟焉而已
哉抑稽昔者舜作五絃之琴以歌南風夔始制
樂以賞諸侯其賞之也一惟視其德之厚薄未
===
嘗至於濫賞下文所謂其治民勞者其舞行綴
遠其治民逸者其舞行綴短槩可見矣噫制樂
不以巳而賞樂因其德此先王之世所以樂必
盡善盡美而觀樂則可以知其德也後世燕奏
肆夏庭舞八佾殆不知此
三代之王也必先其令聞
陸中行
同考試官訓導左批塲中作此題者多不知
punctuated:
之類，各以時熟，而無或愆期，則德之盛於此乎可徵。天子於此，得不賞樂以章其德哉？盖樂有羽旄，夔所制也，于焉錫之以羽旄，以為文舞之用；樂有干戚，夔所制也，于焉錫之以干戚，以充武舞之列。是則樂舞一舉，而侯德以著；綴兆一陳，而侯德以章。先王賞樂於諸侯，豈苟焉而已哉？抑稽昔者，舜作五絃之琴，以歌南風，夔始制樂，以賞諸侯。其賞之也，一惟視其德之厚薄，未嘗至於濫賞。下文所謂「其治民勞者，其舞行綴遠；其治民逸者，其舞行綴短」，槩可見矣。噫！制樂不以巳，而賞樂因其德，此先王之世所以樂必盡善盡美，而觀樂則可以知其德也。後世燕奏肆夏，庭舞八佾，殆不知此。

三代之王也必先其令聞
陸中行
同考試官訓導左批：塲中作此題者，多不知
translation_en:
…and the like each ripen in their proper season, none missing its appointed time: here the fullness of their virtue can be verified. In such circumstances, could the Son of Heaven fail to reward them with music to make their virtue manifest? Musical performances have feather and yak-tail standards, devised by Kui; these are bestowed upon them for use in the civil dance. Musical performances have shields and battle-axes, devised by Kui; these are bestowed upon them to furnish the ranks of the martial dance. Thus, once the music and dance begin, the feudal lord’s virtue is revealed; once the dancers’ positions and boundaries are laid out, his virtue is displayed. Could the former kings’ bestowal of music upon the feudal lords have been merely a casual act?

Consider antiquity: Shun made a five-stringed zither to sing the song “Southern Wind,” and Kui first devised music to reward the feudal lords. These rewards depended solely on the degree of their virtue; they were never bestowed indiscriminately. This can broadly be seen in the passage below: “For those who exert themselves in governing the people, the spacing between the dance ranks is wide; for those who take their ease in governing the people, the spacing between the dance ranks is narrow.” Ah! Music was devised without regard to oneself, and its bestowal depended upon the recipient’s virtue. This is why, in the age of the former kings, music necessarily attained perfect goodness and perfect beauty, and why observing the music made it possible to know their virtue. In later ages, those who performed “Si Xia” at banquets and staged dances in eight ranks in their courtyards seem not to have understood this.

“Those who became kings in the Three Dynasties were invariably preceded by their good reputation.”

Lu Zhongxing

Associate Examiner Zuo, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Many of those who wrote on this topic in the examination hall fail to understand…”

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
旨此篇說出三王無私之德明白簡切非熟於禮不能
也寘諸上第允愜輿情
考試官教諭鄭批文從理順
考試官學正朱批禮經義無有能如此作者
論歷代受命而興由先世著無私之譽也夫三
代之王同一無私而已今聖人又原其先世之
令聞豈無意哉昔聖人因子夏問三王之德參
於天地而告之及此意豈不謂塗山啓會萬國
===
歸心此大禹之王於夏也帝命下臨九圍是式
此成湯之王於商也文王以文治而三分有二
武王以武功而四海永清非文武之王於周乎
三代之王如此夫豈無自而然哉誠以大禹受
命而興非但禹之一身有是無私之德而天遂
命之也蓋未王之先有顓頊爲之祖頊嘗法施
於民其積德之深已有無私之令聞慰服於當
時之人心矣夏之有天下實基於此成湯受命
punctuated:
旨。此篇說出三王無私之德，明白簡切，非熟於禮不能也。寘諸上第，允愜輿情。
考試官教諭鄭批：文從理順。
考試官學正朱批：禮經義，無有能如此作者。
論歷代受命而興，由先世著無私之譽也。夫三代之王，同一無私而已。今聖人又原其先世之令聞，豈無意哉？昔聖人因子夏問三王之德參於天地，而告之及此。意豈不謂塗山啓會，萬國歸心，此大禹之王於夏也；帝命下臨，九圍是式，此成湯之王於商也；文王以文治而三分有二，武王以武功而四海永清，非文武之王於周乎？三代之王如此，夫豈無自而然哉？誠以大禹受命而興，非但禹之一身有是無私之德，而天遂命之也。蓋未王之先，有顓頊爲之祖，頊嘗法施於民，其積德之深，已有無私之令聞，慰服於當時之人心矣。夏之有天下，實基於此。成湯受命
translation_en:
…the meaning. This essay brings out the selfless virtue of the kings of the Three Dynasties clearly, concisely, and directly. Only someone thoroughly versed in the rites could achieve this. Placing it among the highest-ranked essays truly accords with the general judgment.
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “The writing flows naturally, and the reasoning is sound.”
Examiner Zhu, School Instructor, comments: “Among essays interpreting the Classic of Rites, none can match this.”
I maintain that the rulers of successive dynasties received the Mandate and rose to power because their forebears had established a reputation for selflessness. The kings of the Three Dynasties shared one quality: selflessness. Now, when the Sage further traced this back to the good reputation of their forebears, could he have done so without a purpose? When Zixia asked how the virtue of the kings of the Three Dynasties stood alongside Heaven and Earth, the Sage’s answer extended to this point. Surely his meaning was this: the assembly was convened at Tushan, and the myriad states gave their allegiance—such was Yu the Great’s kingship in Xia. The Lord on High’s command descended, and the nine regions took him as their model—such was Cheng Tang’s kingship in Shang. King Wen, through civil governance, possessed two of the realm’s three parts; King Wu, through military achievement, brought lasting peace within the Four Seas. Was this not the kingship of Wen and Wu in Zhou? Such were the kings of the Three Dynasties. Could their achievements have come about without an antecedent cause?
Truly, Yu the Great received the Mandate and rose to power not simply because Yu himself possessed this selfless virtue and Heaven therefore bestowed its Mandate upon him. Before he became king, he had Zhuanxu as his ancestor. Zhuanxu had applied exemplary rules to the people. Through his deeply accumulated virtue, he had already gained a fine reputation for selflessness, reassuring the people of his time and winning their hearts. Xia’s possession of All under Heaven was founded upon this. Cheng Tang received the Mandate…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而興非徒湯之一身有是無私之德而帝遂命
之也盖未王之先有契爲之始祖契嘗敬敷五
敎其積德之厚已有無私之令聞固結於當時
之人心矣商之有天下實肇于兹若夫文武之
興王於周人皆知其有無私之德故天眷之也
殊不知周之先世有后稷敎民稼穡有王季其
勤王家其積功累仁有素矣周之有天下不先
有無私之令聞著于未王之先乎聖人論三代
===
之王而必原其祖宗積德之所自此可見王業
之興其積累非一日矣孰敢以私議之哉抑考
閒居一篇皆聖人答子夏之問始論爲民父母
之道則在於致五至而行三無終論參於天地
之德則在於奉三無私而先令聞盖有爲民父
母之道然後可以行三王之德洪範曰天子作
民父母以爲天下王其序有如是夫
論
punctuated:
而興，非徒湯之一身有是無私之德而帝遂命之也。盖未王之先，有契爲之始祖，契嘗敬敷五敎，其積德之厚，已有無私之令聞固結於當時之人心矣。商之有天下，實肇于兹。若夫文武之興王於周，人皆知其有無私之德，故天眷之也。殊不知周之先世，有后稷敎民稼穡，有王季其勤王家，其積功累仁有素矣。周之有天下，不先有無私之令聞著于未王之先乎？聖人論三代之王，而必原其祖宗積德之所自，此可見王業之興，其積累非一日矣，孰敢以私議之哉？抑考《閒居》一篇，皆聖人答子夏之問。始論爲民父母之道，則在於致五至而行三無；終論參於天地之德，則在於奉三無私而先令聞。盖有爲民父母之道，然後可以行三王之德。《洪範》曰：「天子作民父母，以爲天下王。」其序有如是夫！

論
translation_en:
…and rose to power, it was not merely because Tang himself possessed this virtue of impartiality that the Lord on High thereupon conferred the mandate upon him. Before he became king, there was Xie, the founding ancestor of his line. Xie had reverently disseminated the five teachings. So substantial was his accumulated virtue that his fine reputation for impartiality had already become firmly rooted in the hearts of the people of his time. Shang’s possession of All under Heaven truly originated here. As for Wen and Wu rising to kingship in Zhou, everyone knows that Heaven favored them because they possessed the virtue of impartiality. Yet people fail to realize that among Zhou’s ancestors were Hou Ji, who taught the people to sow and reap, and Wang Ji, who labored diligently for the royal house. Their accumulation of meritorious deeds and benevolence was long established. Before Zhou possessed All under Heaven, had not a fine reputation for impartiality already become manifest, even before its rulers became kings? When the Sage discusses the kingship of the Three Dynasties, he invariably traces it to the virtue accumulated by their ancestors. From this we can see that the rise of a royal enterprise rests on an accumulation extending far beyond a single day. Who would dare characterize it as a matter of partiality?

Furthermore, examining the chapter “At Leisure” (Xianju), we find that it consists entirely of the Sage’s answers to Zixia’s questions. It begins by discussing the way to become father and mother to the people: this lies in bringing the five attainments to fulfillment and practicing the three things without outward form. It ends by discussing how to participate in the virtue of Heaven and Earth: this lies in honoring the three forms of impartiality and establishing a fine reputation beforehand. Only after possessing the way to become father and mother to the people can one put into practice the virtue of the Three Kings. The “Great Plan” (Hongfan) says: “The Son of Heaven becomes father and mother to the people, thereby becoming king of All under Heaven.” Such indeed is the proper sequence!

Discourses

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
帝王之治一本於道
謝慶
同考試官訓導湯批有發揮有指歸論之優者
考試官教諭鄭批舂容大篇能闡明帝王之道
者此作見之
考試官學正朱批詞富而理明當是作家用魁多
士何忝
論曰帝王之致治也豈有他哉亦曰道而
===
已蓋道乃為治之本也治而本於道則近
而一家家以之而齊遠而一國國以之而
治極其遠而天下天下以之而平矣苟為
不然則徒操為治之柄而失為治之本欲
家國天下之治平也不其難乎愚嘗伏讀
太宗文皇帝御製性理大全序文有曰帝王之
治一本於道大哉
皇言乎一哉
punctuated:
帝王之治一本於道

謝慶

同考試官訓導湯批：有發揮，有指歸，論之優者。

考試官教諭鄭批：舂容大篇，能闡明帝王之道者，此作見之。

考試官學正朱批：詞富而理明，當是作家，用魁多士何忝？

論曰：帝王之致治也，豈有他哉？亦曰道而已。蓋道乃為治之本也。治而本於道，則近而一家，家以之而齊；遠而一國，國以之而治；極其遠而天下，天下以之而平矣。苟為不然，則徒操為治之柄，而失為治之本，欲家國天下之治平也，不其難乎？愚嘗伏讀太宗文皇帝御製《性理大全》序文，有曰：「帝王之治，一本於道。」大哉，皇言乎！一哉，
translation_en:
The Governance of Emperors and Kings Is Rooted Entirely in the Way

Xie Qing

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Assistant Instructor: There is elaboration, and there is a clear direction to the argument. This is an outstanding discourse.

Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: A capacious, unhurried composition. Here we see a work capable of elucidating the Way of emperors and kings.

Comment by Examiner Zhu, Instructor: Rich in expression and clear in principle: surely the work of an accomplished writer. What cause for shame could there be in placing it foremost among the many candidates?

The discourse reads: Is there anything else by which emperors and kings bring about good government? It is simply the Way. For the Way is the foundation of governance. When governance is rooted in the Way, in the nearest sphere—the family—the family is thereby set in order; in the more distant sphere—the state—the state is thereby well governed; and in the most distant sphere—all under Heaven—all under Heaven is thereby brought to peace. If this is not so, one merely holds the instruments of government while losing its foundation. Would it not then be difficult to attain order and peace in the family, the state, and all under Heaven?

I have humbly read Emperor Taizong Wen’s imperially composed preface to the Great Compendium of Human Nature and Principle (Xingli daquan), which says: “The governance of emperors and kings is rooted entirely in the Way.” How great are these imperial words! How single-minded…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
皇心乎其真知帝王為治之本乎且帝王之生
豈偶然哉膺上天付託之重任斯民君師
之責九重之上萬化之攸繫焉一日之間
萬幾之紛至焉禮樂刑政於此而脩舉井
田學校於此而制立民吾同胞而民之衆
也由我以子育物吾同與而物之多也由
我以生遂天地之財成本於我化育之參
賛本於我九夷八蠻之勞來而撫綏也本
===
於我所係為甚重也所關為甚大也將欲
治之以智耶智有窮而天下之大無窮智
豈為治之本乎抑欲治之以力耶力有限
而天下之大也無限力豈為治之本乎若
此者舉不足以言治然則帝王之致治也
非是道而何歟夫所謂道者原於天而具
於人具於人而根於心非高遠而難行也
非驚世而駭俗也求之人倫日用常行之
punctuated: 皇心乎！其真知帝王為治之本乎！且帝王之生，豈偶然哉？膺上天付託之重，任斯民君師之責，九重之上，萬化之攸繫焉；一日之間，萬幾之紛至焉。禮樂刑政於此而脩舉，井田學校於此而制立。民吾同胞，而民之衆也，由我以子育；物吾同與，而物之多也，由我以生遂。天地之財成本於我，化育之參賛本於我，九夷八蠻之勞來而撫綏也本於我。所係為甚重也，所關為甚大也。將欲治之以智耶？智有窮，而天下之大無窮，智豈為治之本乎？抑欲治之以力耶？力有限，而天下之大也無限，力豈為治之本乎？若此者，舉不足以言治。然則帝王之致治也，非是道而何歟？夫所謂道者，原於天而具於人，具於人而根於心，非高遠而難行也，非驚世而駭俗也，求之人倫日用常行之
translation_en: …the imperial mind! Does he not truly understand the foundation upon which emperors and kings govern? Moreover, could the birth of an emperor or king be a mere accident? He bears the weighty trust bestowed by Heaven and assumes responsibility as ruler and teacher of the people. High within the ninefold palace, he is the one upon whom all transformations depend; within a single day, the myriad affairs of government crowd upon him. Through him, rites, music, punishments, and administration are cultivated and put into effect; through him, the well-field system and schools are instituted. The people are my siblings, and their multitudes depend upon me to nurture them as children; all things are my companions, and their abundance depends upon me to enable them to live and flourish. Regulating and bringing to completion the work of Heaven and Earth depends upon me; assisting their transforming and nurturing powers depends upon me; comforting, attracting, and pacifying the Nine Yi and Eight Man peoples depends upon me. What rests upon him is exceedingly weighty; what is at stake is exceedingly great. Would he govern through cleverness? Cleverness is exhaustible, whereas the vastness of all under Heaven is inexhaustible. How could cleverness be the foundation of government? Or would he govern through force? Force has limits, whereas the vastness of all under Heaven is limitless. How could force be the foundation of government? Such means are altogether inadequate as a basis for discussing government. If so, by what other than this Way can emperors and kings bring about good government? What is called the Way originates in Heaven and is fully present in human beings; fully present in human beings, it is rooted in the heart. It is neither lofty and remote, difficult to practice, nor something that shocks the world and startles ordinary people. Seek it amid human relationships and the customary practices of daily life…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
間則可見矣是故親也義也父子君臣之
道也親義之道行於上殆見人同此心而
天下之爲父子君臣者必是則是效同一
有親而有義矣别也序也信也夫婦長幼
朋友之道也序别信之道篤於上殆見人
同此理而天下之爲夫婦長幼朋友者必
是矜是式同一有别有序而有信矣道乃
天之經也天經正則萬化以之而行道乃
===
地之義也地義立則萬變以之而出由是
以制禮作樂則大禮與天地同節大樂與
天地同和禮樂其有不興乎由是以賞善
罰惡則賞一人而千萬人說罰一人而千
萬人懼刑罰其有不中乎制田里以養民
而民生之厚是道有以厚之也立學校以
教民而民性之復是道有以復之也施於
政而達於事者莫非是道之發越篤於近
punctuated: 間，則可見矣。是故親也，義也，父子君臣之道也。親義之道行於上，殆見人同此心，而天下之爲父子君臣者，必是則是效，同一有親而有義矣。别也，序也，信也，夫婦長幼朋友之道也。序别信之道篤於上，殆見人同此理，而天下之爲夫婦長幼朋友者，必是矜是式，同一有别有序而有信矣。道乃天之經也，天經正，則萬化以之而行；道乃地之義也，地義立，則萬變以之而出。由是以制禮作樂，則大禮與天地同節，大樂與天地同和，禮樂其有不興乎？由是以賞善罰惡，則賞一人而千萬人說，罰一人而千萬人懼，刑罰其有不中乎？制田里以養民，而民生之厚，是道有以厚之也；立學校以教民，而民性之復，是道有以復之也。施於政而達於事者，莫非是道之發越；篤於近
translation_en:
…amid these, it can be perceived. Thus affection and righteousness are the Way governing fathers and sons, rulers and ministers. When the Way of affection and righteousness is practiced by those above, we may expect to see that all people share this same heart: throughout the realm, fathers and sons, rulers and ministers will surely take this as their standard and example, alike possessing affection and righteousness. Distinction, precedence, and trustworthiness are the Way governing husbands and wives, elders and juniors, and friends. When those above earnestly uphold the Way of precedence, distinction, and trustworthiness, we may expect to see that all people share this same principle: throughout the realm, husbands and wives, elders and juniors, and friends will surely take this as their model and pattern, alike observing distinction, precedence, and trustworthiness.

The Way is Heaven’s constant norm. When Heaven’s norm is set right, all transformations proceed through it. The Way is Earth’s proper order. When Earth’s order is established, all changes emerge through it. If rites are instituted and music composed on this basis, the great rites accord with the measures of Heaven and Earth, and great music accords with their harmony. How could rites and music fail to flourish? If good is rewarded and evil punished on this basis, rewarding one person will gladden thousands upon thousands, and punishing one person will make thousands upon thousands fearful. How could punishments fail to be fitting? When fields and settlements are organized to nourish the people and their livelihoods become abundant, it is this Way that makes them abundant. When schools are established to teach the people and their original nature is restored, it is this Way that restores it. Whatever is applied in government and carried through in affairs is an expression of this Way; what is earnestly practiced among those near at hand…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而舉於遠者莫非是道之流通所以財成
天地者本於此所以叅賛化育者本於此
所以撫九夷而綏八蠻者本於此是則帝
王之治天下其所以致雍熈悠乆之盛者
誠不外於此道矣區區之知力烏可與道
同日而語哉雖然此道也聖人未生具在
天地聖人既生具在聖人聖人既往具在
六經六經也者斯道之攸寓也六經之教
===
===
明於天下斯道之明於天下也其日之中
天乎六經之教行於萬世斯道之行於萬
世也其水之行地乎帝王之生有先後道
不以先後而或殊世運之興有古今道不
以古今而或間千載之下遐陬僻壤疆域
雖不同而同此父子親君臣義者誰之功
斯道之功也百世之遠深山窮谷地勢雖
不同而同此夫婦別長幼序朋友信者誰
punctuated: 而舉於遠者，莫非是道之流通。所以財成天地者本於此，所以叅賛化育者本於此，所以撫九夷而綏八蠻者本於此。是則帝王之治天下，其所以致雍熈悠乆之盛者，誠不外於此道矣。區區之知力，烏可與道同日而語哉！雖然，此道也，聖人未生，具在天地；聖人既生，具在聖人；聖人既往，具在六經。六經也者，斯道之攸寓也。六經之教明於天下，斯道之明於天下也，其日之中天乎！六經之教行於萬世，斯道之行於萬世也，其水之行地乎！帝王之生有先後，道不以先後而或殊；世運之興有古今，道不以古今而或間。千載之下，遐陬僻壤，疆域雖不同，而同此父子親、君臣義者，誰之功？斯道之功也。百世之遠，深山窮谷，地勢雖不同，而同此夫婦別、長幼序、朋友信者，誰
translation_en:
…and whatever is extended to those far away is likewise the circulation of this Way. It is the foundation for ordering and bringing to completion the work of Heaven and Earth, for assisting their transforming and nurturing powers, and for pacifying the Nine Yi and bringing tranquility to the Eight Man. Thus, when emperors and kings govern All under Heaven, the means by which they achieve flourishing harmony and enduring prosperity truly lie entirely within this Way. How could mere knowledge and effort be mentioned in the same breath as the Way!

Nevertheless, before the sages were born, this Way was fully present in Heaven and Earth; once the sages were born, it was fully present in the sages; after the sages had passed away, it was fully present in the Six Classics. The Six Classics are where this Way resides. When the teachings of the Six Classics shine throughout All under Heaven, this Way shines throughout All under Heaven: is it not like the sun at the zenith? When the teachings of the Six Classics are practiced through ten thousand generations, this Way is practiced through ten thousand generations: is it not like water flowing over the earth? Emperors and kings are born at different times, but the Way does not differ on account of their coming earlier or later. The unfolding fortunes of the world belong to ancient or modern times, but the Way suffers no interruption on account of that distinction. A thousand years later, in distant corners and remote regions, although territorial boundaries differ, affection between father and son and righteousness between ruler and minister remain the same. Whose achievement is this? It is the achievement of this Way. A hundred generations removed, in deep mountains and secluded valleys, although the terrain differs, distinction between husband and wife, precedence between older and younger, and trustworthiness between friends remain the same—whose…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之力斯道之力也由是觀之帝王之有天
下固不外是道以求治亦豈外六經以求
道歟稽之於古伏羲神農黃帝之世渾渾
然噩噩然道之寓於治也無迹而可見自
是而後堯之親睦九族舜之慎徽五典非
二帝之治一本於道乎禹之祗台德先湯
之肇脩人紀文王之緝熈敬止武王之皇
建有極非三王之治一本於道乎下及漢
===
唐之君或忽之而不行或行之而不純是
以或治或否或久或近率不能如古昔之
盛而人不得蒙至治之澤者夫豈無其故
道之不明不行故也三皇遠矣二帝三王
往矣秦漢以下諸君不足言矣洪惟我
朝
太祖高皇帝受天景命奄有萬方以身而體道
以道而致治
punctuated:
之力？斯道之力也。由是觀之，帝王之有天下，固不外是道以求治，亦豈外六經以求道歟？稽之於古，伏羲、神農、黃帝之世，渾渾然，噩噩然，道之寓於治也，無迹而可見。自是而後，堯之親睦九族，舜之慎徽五典，非二帝之治一本於道乎？禹之祗台德先，湯之肇脩人紀，文王之緝熈敬止，武王之皇建有極，非三王之治一本於道乎？下及漢唐之君，或忽之而不行，或行之而不純，是以或治或否，或久或近，率不能如古昔之盛，而人不得蒙至治之澤者，夫豈無其故？道之不明不行故也。
三皇遠矣，二帝三王往矣，秦漢以下諸君不足言矣。洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝，受天景命，奄有萬方，以身而體道，以道而致治。
translation_en:
…whose achievement is this? It is the achievement of this Way. Viewed thus, when emperors and kings possess All under Heaven, they assuredly do not seek good government outside this Way; how, then, could they seek the Way outside the Six Classics? Examining antiquity, we find that in the ages of Fuxi, Shennong, and the Yellow Emperor, all was simple and uncontrived: the Way was embodied in government without any visible trace. Thereafter, Yao brought the nine degrees of kinship into loving harmony, and Shun carefully promoted the five cardinal teachings. Was not the government of these Two Emperors rooted entirely in the Way? Yu reverently put his own virtue first; Tang began to cultivate the ordering of human relationships; King Wen maintained luminous virtue and rested in reverence; and King Wu grandly established the supreme standard. Was not the government of the Three Kings rooted entirely in the Way? Coming down to the rulers of Han and Tang, some neglected it and failed to practice it, while others practiced it without purity. Consequently, some achieved order and others did not; some endured long and others only briefly. Generally, they could not equal the flourishing government of antiquity, and the people could not enjoy the blessings of perfect government. Could this have been without a cause? It was because the Way was neither made clear nor put into practice.
The Three Sovereigns are distant indeed; the Two Emperors and Three Kings have passed away. The rulers from Qin and Han onward are scarcely worth discussing. We reverently reflect that Emperor Taizu Gao of our dynasty received Heaven’s great mandate and possessed all the myriad regions. In his own person he embodied the Way, and through the Way he achieved good government…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
列聖相承孜孜圖治闡明六經之教昭示五倫
之道百二十餘年
皇風清穆治化休明足以肩二帝超三王而
衍億萬年無疆之
盛治非區區漢唐所可及也然則帝王之治
一本於道正在
今日愚何幸躬逢其
盛
===
表
擬宋以唐介參知政事謝表熙寧元年
張紹齡
同考試官訓導黃批表麗則
考試官教諭鄭批表豐贍
考試官學正朱批表得體
伏以
金鼎調元絲綸密勿之地
punctuated:
列聖相承，孜孜圖治，闡明六經之教，昭示五倫之道。百二十餘年，皇風清穆，治化休明，足以肩二帝、超三王，而衍億萬年無疆之盛治，非區區漢唐所可及也。然則帝王之治，一本於道，正在今日。愚何幸躬逢其盛！

表
擬宋以唐介參知政事謝表，熙寧元年。
張紹齡
同考試官訓導黃批：表麗則。
考試官教諭鄭批：表豐贍。
考試官學正朱批：表得體。

伏以：金鼎調元，絲綸密勿之地，
translation_en:
…Successive sage emperors have carried on the succession, working tirelessly for good government, elucidating the teachings of the Six Classics and clearly revealing the Way of the Five Human Relationships. For more than 120 years, imperial influence has been pure and harmonious, and government and moral transformation splendid and enlightened. This is sufficient to rival the Two Emperors, surpass the Three Kings, and extend the boundless flourishing of good government for countless ages. The merely modest achievements of the Han and Tang cannot compare. Thus, government by emperors and kings, rooted wholly in the Way, is realized precisely in our own day. How fortunate I, in my ignorance, am to encounter this flourishing age in person!

Memorial
A simulated memorial of thanks for the Song appointment of Tang Jie as Participant in Determining Governmental Matters, in the first year of Xining [1068].
By Zhang Shaoling.
Associate Examiner Huang, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The memorial is elegant and conforms to proper standards.”
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “The memorial is rich and ample.”
Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “The memorial accords with the appropriate form.”

I humbly submit: To harmonize the primal forces in the golden cauldron—the office where imperial pronouncements are diligently and confidentially prepared…

title: 成化二十二年廣東鄉試錄
text:
玉宸贊化鈞衡崇峻之階詎意凡庸遽蒙拔
擢端拜
白麻之寵與參紫府之班
恩命自天汗容無地茲蓋伏遇
〇〇〇〇
道同坤厚
德配乾剛於昭不顯之誠用建維皇之極恭

Reverently ordering yourself, you practice diligence and frugality; in serving your parents, you display pure filial devotion and benevolence. Emulating your ancestors and revering Heaven, you are truly a ruler rarely seen through the ages; seeking worthy men and striving for good government, you are indeed a sovereign capable of great achievements. Outstanding men fill the court, all wholeheartedly assisting your great transforming work; the aged and the young crowd the roads, all eagerly watching for the sight of peace. Historians record your achievements without cease, and everyone’s hopes are fulfilled. You employ men as one employs medicines, overlooking neither puffballs [?] nor ox urine; you select scholars as one selects materials—would you discard even bamboo ends and wood shavings?

translation_en:
…in the former reign, I undeservedly held a remonstrating office and hoped to exert myself in making subtle matters manifest [?]. Because I attacked the private interests of the chief councillors, intent on cleansing the administration, and spoke with uprightness and pointed candor, I was sent out to serve as Adjutant of Yingzhou. I willingly accepted banishment to the wilderness with what little breath remained to me. Returning alive to serve the altars of soil and grain, I had already lost hope of a place among the court’s literary scholars; escaping the storms of a perilous course, I had not forgotten my verses on the banks of the Huai. My service at court had never benefited this enlightened age, and my discussions of affairs repeatedly ran counter to prevailing opinion. Reflecting on my lot, I thought it fitting that I should die and fill a ditch. Yet Heaven’s grace did not discard even such humble greens as I: I was raised from the margins of idle retirement and appointed deputy to the chief councillor. This distinction lay beyond anything I had imagined; favor and anxiety arrived together.
How could your servant fail to sharpen his capacities for planning and action and invigorate his integrity? Through exchanges of assent and dissent, I would join in the answering songs of the age of Shun; invoking blessings, emoluments, longevity, and well-being, I would emulate the indirect remonstrance of the poem “Winding Hills” (Juan e). Diligent at dawn and diligent at night, I would reverently expend all my strength in loyal service, like a dog or horse. Careful at the beginning and careful at the end, I would repay the virtue of Heaven and Earth above.
I humbly wish that your imperial influence may be pure and harmonious and your imperial virtue radiant; that you may perpetuate the glories of this illustrious age and richly bestow blessings upon the common people. May your sunlike brilliance illuminate all, as all alike gaze upon the sun…

translation_en:
…throughout the realm, showing that the hearts of all within the four seas share a single principle; laws handed down to later generations show that the institutions fashioned by the successive sage rulers express a single intent. This likewise informed the instructions and proclamations composed by the rulers of Shang and Zhou. When the statutes of our dynasty’s successive sage rulers are compared with those instructions and proclamations, they agree in every respect. Is this not the reason? Allow me to set forth one or two points in response to your illuminating question.
August Heaven, the Lord on High, bestowed an upright disposition upon the people below; in following it, they possess a constant nature. Thus what Heaven ordains contains goodness and no evil. Yet desires stir and feelings prevail; considerations of gain and harm clash, and evil arises. A sage must therefore emerge, occupy the position of ruler and teacher, and shoulder responsibility for government and instruction. Embodying Heaven in bringing about good government, he makes goodness manifest and chastises evil, leading the people of the realm to turn toward goodness and abandon evil, earnestly uphold ethical relationships, and help bring governance and moral transformation to their flourishing culmination. From antiquity, all emperors and kings have acted thus. Let us take the rulers of Shang and Zhou as examples. When Cheng Tang proclaimed his message far and wide, he said: “All of you who establish our states: do not follow what contravenes constant norms, nor fall into wanton excess. Each of you must uphold your established rules, thereby receiving Heaven’s blessings.” His intent to encourage and admonish is abundantly clear. When King Cheng instructed and guided the officials, he said: “All of you who hold office in our service …

translation_en:
…gentlemen, attend reverently to your responsibilities and exercise care in issuing commands. Let public duty overcome private interests, and the people will surely cherish you.” The intent to encourage and admonish is abundantly clear. Thus Shang’s myriad people truly flourished, and Zhou’s myriad states remained unwearied in their allegiance. The splendid results of their government could not be surpassed.
We reverently reflect that, in our dynasty, Emperor Taizu Gao established his rule over the Chinese realm; Emperor Taizong Wen magnificently carried forward his grand designs; and Emperor Xuanzong Zhang brought peace to the state. These three sages succeeded one another, and institutions and regulations became fully developed. Among the works determined by their imperial judgment and promulgated throughout the realm were the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao), Doing Good and Hidden Virtue (Weishan Yinzhi), True Accounts of Filial Obedience (Xiaoshun Shishi), and the Book of the Five Relationships (Wulun Shu). Their imperial writings illuminate heaven and earth. In graciously benefiting officials and people, they are supremely refined and comprehensive: truly great canons that shall remain unaltered for ten thousand generations. When I, in my humble ignorance, solemnly recite and reverently examine them, I find provisions encouraging goodness recurring across the compilations, and categories for punishing evil appearing in their respective illustrative cases. The Grand Pronouncements says, “Serve your ruler with loyalty.” The loyal achievements of Han Qi recorded in Hidden Virtue, the loyalty and filial devotion of Zhao Bian recorded in True Accounts, and the Five…

translation_en: …the Book of the Five Relationships says, “Serving one’s ruler according to righteousness is called loyalty.” Does this not share a common thread and underlying principle with Cheng Tang’s proclamation, “Each of you must uphold your prescribed duties”? The Grand Pronouncements says, “Discharge official duties with reverence.” Fan Zhongyan’s fulfillment of his duties, recorded in Good Deeds and Hidden Virtue; Cui Xuanwei’s faithful discharge of office, recorded in Accounts of Filial Piety and Obedience; and “upholding the law and benefiting the people,” as stated in the Book of the Five Relationships—do these not accord perfectly with King Cheng’s injunction, “Be reverent in what you administer”? The writings of the three sage emperors are no different from those of the former kings; the government of the three sage emperors is no different from that of the former kings. Thus, upon succeeding to the imperial throne, our Emperor has taken the Way of Shang and Zhou as his distant model and upheld the laws of his imperial ancestors as his nearer guide. When he commends people’s goodness, even a cold valley is warmed by spring; when he corrects people’s wickedness, startling frost falls in summer. Throughout all beneath Heaven, everyone sees goodness encouraged, yet does not know whose action brings about that encouragement; everyone sees evil punished, yet does not know whose power brings about that punishment. The Classic says, “Take King Wen as your model.” The Commentary says, “There has never been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and went astray.” Could one then say that the government of today is not clear proof of the continuing illumination of sagely learning and adherence to the established statutes? 知作史之難，則秉筆者不容以或易；知評史之難，則持論者不可以或輕。何也？盖作史者，所以著歷代之得失；評史者，又所以明秉筆之是非。秉筆不公，則得失不可得而考；持論不公，則是非不可得而定。此遷、固二史所以不能免於君子之評，而宜有以廑執事之問也。請條陳之。粵自書契既
